title: Mathematics for DSA and Competitive Programming
relevance: Integer overflow, modular arithmetic, GCD/LCM, sieves, and fast exponentiation are staple OA/interview tools for digit, prime, and combinatorics problems.

phases.goal: Establish C++ integer arithmetic pitfalls and basic digit/number problem patterns.

must_hit.point: In C++, integer division truncates toward zero and % takes the sign of the dividend (e.g., -5/2 is -2 and -5%2 is -1).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both truncation-toward-zero and dividend-signed modulo with the negative examples.

must_hit.point: Use long long for products or sums that might exceed 10^9, and append LL to literals when shifting or multiplying (e.g., 1LL<<32) because literals default to int.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions long long for large products/sums and LL-suffixed literals for shifts/multiplies.

must_hit.point: Digit count can be done by repeated /10, by floor(log10(n))+1, or by converting to a string and taking its size (with a special case for n==0).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the three approaches and the zero edge case.

must_hit.point: Negatives are never palindromes; numbers ending in 0 (except 0) are not either; optimal palindrome check reverses only half the digits.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Covers negative/trailing-zero rejection and half-reverse comparison including odd-length /10.

probes: What goes wrong with a%m when a is negative in C++, and how do you get a non-negative residue?
How would you reverse a signed 32-bit integer without overflowing?

hints.1: Think about sign of % and when rev*10 can exceed INT_MAX/INT_MIN.
hints.2: Positive modulo uses (a%m+m)%m; reverse checks bounds before multiplying by 10.
hints.3: Cite -5%2==-1, the (a%m+m)%m fix, and pre-multiply checks against INT_MAX/10 with pop>7 and INT_MIN/10 with pop<-8.

phases.goal: Explain how Euclidean GCD/LCM, sqrt-n divisor/prime tricks, sieves, and modular ops actually work.

must_hit.point: Euclidean GCD uses gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,a%b); LCM follows from a*b=gcd*lcm, computed as (a/gcd)*b to avoid overflow.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the Euclidean recurrence and overflow-safe LCM formula.

must_hit.point: Divisors and trial primality only need iteration up to sqrt(n) because divisors come in pairs (i and n/i).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains the pair trick and why the loop bound is i*i<=n.

must_hit.point: Sieve of Eratosthenes marks multiples of each prime starting from its square; SPF precompute then factorizes each query in O(log n) after O(n log log n) build.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes marking from i*i and SPF giving O(log n) per factorization.

must_hit.point: Binary exponentiation computes a^b mod m in O(log b) by squaring; modular inverse for prime m is binpow(b,m-2,m) via Fermat.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links even/odd binary exp recurrence to Fermat inverse as b^(m-2).

probes: Walk through Euclidean GCD and how you safely get LCM from it.
How does an SPF sieve turn many factorizations into O(log n) each?

hints.1: Recall the remainder step and what you store instead of a boolean sieve.
hints.2: gcd via repeated %; SPF[i] is the smallest prime dividing i, then peel factors.
hints.3: gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,a%b); lcm=(a/gcd)*b; after SPF build in O(n log log n), while n!=1 push spf[n] and divide.

phases.goal: Compare approaches candidates choose under different constraints and correctness needs.

must_hit.point: Cast before multiplying: assigning a*b to long long still overflows if both are int and the product exceeds 2*10^9; use (long long)a*b.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States intermediate int multiply overflows even when the destination is long long.

must_hit.point: For many factorizations prefer SPF sieve over per-query O(sqrt(n)) trial division; for range primes with small R (up to 10^7) use sieve+prefix, but large L,R with small R-L need a segmented sieve.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts SPF vs trial and standard sieve+prefix vs segmented sieve by constraint.

must_hit.point: nCr mod p via precomputed factorials and inverse factorials beats Pascal for large n; Pascal's identity still fits DP under small constraints.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says factorial+inverse is faster for large n while Pascal helps small DP.

probes: When do you pick SPF over plain trial factorization?
Why is nCr via factorials preferred over building Pascal's triangle in OAs?

hints.1: Think one-shot vs many queries, and size of n vs need for DP.
hints.2: Precompute once when many numbers share a bound; Pascal grows with n and r.
hints.3: SPF: O(n log log n) then O(log n)/query; factorial inverses for large nCr mod p, Pascal when constraints are small and DP-shaped.

phases.goal: Apply the toolkit to typical OA/interview asks and avoid common failure modes.

must_hit.point: Apply modulo at every step; for subtraction use ((a%m)-(b%m)+m)%m; 10^9+7 is prime and fits in 32-bit signed int but products need long long.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recites per-step mod, subtract-with-+m, and 10^9+7 product needing 64-bit.

must_hit.point: pow(x,n) must handle negative exponents via reciprocal and cast n to long long before abs because n=INT_MIN overflows 32-bit negation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions reciprocal for negatives and INT_MIN via long long.

must_hit.point: Interviews/OAs frequently hit GCD/LCM, standard sieve, modpow, combinatorics modulo p, and overflow discipline; Möbius inversion and advanced Diophantine equations virtually never appear.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the frequent topics and explicitly excludes olympiad-heavy theory.

probes: Implement a^b mod m and explain why you mod after every multiply.
What number-theory topics should you prepare for SDE OAs versus skip?

hints.1: Focus on overflow of intermediate products and the interview shortlist.
hints.2: Binary exp with %m each multiply; prep sieve/modpow/nCr, skip Möbius-level theory.
hints.3: binpow loops with (res*a)%m and (a*a)%m; expect GCD/LCM, sieve, modpow, nCr mod p, overflow care—not Möbius or hard Diophantine.

tradeoffs.topic: Digit count: iterative /10 vs log10 vs string
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Iterative division is O(log10 n); log and string conversion are O(1) for fixed 32-bit ints (string uses O(log10 n) space). String is often the most convenient in C++.

tradeoffs.topic: Palindrome: full reverse vs half reverse
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Reversing the whole int risks overflow; reversing only half until reversedHalf>=x avoids overflow and still compares correctly (use reversedHalf/10 for odd length).

tradeoffs.topic: Factorization: trial O(sqrt(n)) vs SPF sieve
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Single query: trial-divide to sqrt(n). Many queries up to n: precompute SPF in O(n log log n) then factorize each in O(log n).

tradeoffs.topic: Range primes: full sieve+prefix vs segmented sieve
tradeoffs.strong_answer: If R is up to 10^7, sieve to R and prefix for O(1) queries. If R is about 10^12 but R-L is small, use a segmented sieve.
Precompute factorials and modular inverses for large n under mod p; use Pascal identity nCr=(n-1)Cr+(n-1)C(r-1) when DP fits small constraints.

tradeoffs.topic: Rolling your own GCD vs std::gcd
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Euclidean is the standard algorithm, but prefer std::gcd (C++17) or std::__gcd from <numeric> over hand-rolled code.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a%m is always in [0,m-1] for negative a in C++.
gotchas.correction: Negative a yields a negative remainder; use (a%m+m)%m for a non-negative residue.

gotchas.trap: Writing long long x = a * b with a and b as int.
gotchas.correction: The int multiply overflows before the assignment if the product exceeds 2*10^9; cast first: (long long)a * b.

gotchas.trap: Only taking modulo at the end of a long computation.
gotchas.correction: Apply % at every step; for subtraction add m before % to avoid negatives.

gotchas.trap: Negating n when implementing pow(x,n) if n is INT_MIN.
gotchas.correction: Cast n to long long before taking the absolute value, then reciprocal the base for negative exponents.

gotchas.trap: Preparing Möbius inversion or advanced Diophantine equations for SDE interviews.
gotchas.correction: Those virtually never appear; focus on GCD/LCM, sieve, modpow, combinatorics mod p, and overflow discipline.
